response.query: Which causal-identification designs (valid instrument candidates, cluster randomization, encouragement designs, stepped-wedge trials) are feasible to disentangle virtue effects from selection in academic settings?
response.answer: Stepped-wedge cluster randomization and encouragement designs are feasible to disentangle virtue effects from selection in academic settings. They allow gradual intervention rollout and account for time-varying effects.

results.title: Stepped-Wedge Designs - Rethinking Clinical Trials
results.content: In stepped-wedge designs, the clusters are randomized into several groups or waves that define when the intervention will begin, and all clusters start the trial in the control condition. As of 2022, all of the NIH Pragmatic Trials Collaboratory Trials that used a stepped-wedge design were granted a waiver of consent (Federico et al 2022). Because of the staggered schedule of intervention rollout in the stepped-wedge design, this regulatory pause introduced a significant disruption to the trial’s implementation, and the researchers speculated that parallel randomization might have been better. results.title: Adherence to key recommendations for design and analysis of stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials: A review of trials published 2016-2022 - PubMed
results.content: # Adherence to key recommendations for design and analysis of stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials: A review of trials published 2016-2022. * 2 Department of Biostatistics, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, USA. * 3 Yale Center for Analytical Sciences, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, USA. # Adherence to key recommendations for design and analysis of stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials: A review of trials published 2016-2022. * 2 Department of Biostatistics, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, USA. * 3 Yale Center for Analytical Sciences, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, USA. **Background/aims:** The stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial (SW-CRT), in which clusters are randomized to a time at which they will transition to the intervention condition - rather than a trial arm - is a relatively new design. To inform future methodological development, including guidance for trialists and the selection of parameters for statistical simulation studies, we conducted a review of recently published SW-CRTs. Specific objectives were to describe (1) the types of designs used in practice, (2) adherence to key requirements for statistical analysis, and (3) practices around covariate adjustment. **Methods:** We used electronic searches to identify primary reports of SW-CRTs published 2016-2022. Many trials had complex design features such as multiple or multivariate primary outcomes (50, 31%) or time-dependent repeated measures (27, 22%). Adherence to some key methodological requirements (adjusting for time effects, accounting for within-period correlation) was higher among trials published in higher versus lower impact factor journals. **Conclusions:** Future methods development should prioritize methods for SW-CRTs with binary or time-to-event outcomes, small numbers of clusters, continuous recruitment designs, multivariate outcomes, or time-dependent repeated measures. Trialists, journal editors, and peer reviewers should be aware that SW-CRTs have additional methodological requirements over parallel arm designs including the need to account for period effects as well as complex intracluster correlations.
